title: Cardi B, Meek Mill, Lil Uzi Vert & More Fuel the Atlantic’s Hustle & Grit: See the Movement Mix
summary: From New York swagger to Philly determination, Billboard and Planet Fitness soundtrack the Atlantic region’s drive with a mix informed by Luminate listening data
contentText:
Along the Atlantic, movement has its own rhythm—from New York’s relentless pace and Philadelphia’s determination to New Jersey’s energy and Virginia’s musical innovation. It’s a region where hustle and grit aren’t just ideas; they’re embedded in the culture and the music that comes from it. 

That spirit drives the  Atlantic Flow Movement Mix , part of the Planet Fitness Movement Mixes exploring the music that keeps people moving. Curated by Billboard’s editorial team and informed by Luminate streaming and consumption data from the region’s top 200 tracks from January 2026 to present, the playlist pairs what Atlantic listeners are playing now with songs that reflect the region’s musical DNA. 

The result moves across hip-hop, pop and dance—from Cardi B and Pop Smoke’s New York energy to Meek Mill and Lil Uzi Vert’s Philly drive and Missy Elliott’s Virginia-born innovation. Different sounds and generations, connected by the same thing: music that makes you want to move, push harder and keep going.

The Spins — Mac Miller , Empire of the Sun

“The Spins” captures Mac Miller at his most youthful and freewheeling, pairing a bright, instantly infectious sample with an easygoing flow. The production feels light on its feet, while Mac’s delivery brings an effortless confidence that keeps the track moving. More than a decade later, that combination still gives the record its feel-good lift.

Public Service Announcement (Interlude) — JAY-Z

Few records communicate confidence as efficiently as “Public Service Announcement.” Just Blaze builds the track around a dramatic, soul-driven beat that feels larger with every bar, while JAY-Z delivers with measured precision. There’s no rush to the performance—its power comes from control, creating the feeling of someone completely certain of his place in the room.

AH HA — Cardi B

Cardi B attacks “AH HA” with the sharp delivery, humor and bravado that have become signatures of her sound. The production gives her plenty of room to punch through, with a hard-edged rhythm that keeps the record tense and propulsive. Cardi’s personality does the rest, turning every bar into an extension of the track’s confrontational energy.

Beauty and a Beat — Justin Bieber featuring Nicki Minaj

“Beauty and a Beat” is pure pop maximalism. Bright synths, electronic drums and an enormous chorus give the track its rush, while Justin Bieber’s melodic delivery keeps it light and buoyant. Nicki Minaj arrives with a playful verse that adds another jolt of personality before the song launches back into its dance-floor pulse.

Dreams and Nightmares (Intro) — Meek Mill

“Dreams and Nightmares (Intro)” is defined by transformation. Meek Mill begins over a sparse, reflective piano progression before the production abruptly shifts and his delivery erupts with it. That transition—from measured reflection to full-throttle release—is what gives the record its lasting power, turning mounting tension into pure adrenaline.

Plain Jane — A$AP Ferg

“Plain Jane” thrives on minimalism. Its hypnotic production leaves space for A$AP Ferg’s clipped, rhythmic delivery to become part of the beat itself. Repetition creates momentum rather than slowing it down, giving the record a steady, almost mechanical drive that makes it easy to lock into.

Promiscuous — Nelly Furtado featuring Timbaland

“Promiscuous” is built around chemistry and rhythm. Timbaland’s production is sparse but deeply percussive, allowing the back-and-forth between him and Nelly Furtado to function almost like another instrument. Playful, flirtatious and constantly in motion, the track proves how much energy can come from groove alone.

Just Wanna Rock — Lil Uzi Vert

“Just Wanna Rock” wastes little time getting to the point. Built around the rapid pulse of Jersey club, the track favors repetition, percussion and physical energy over a traditional verse-chorus structure. Lil Uzi Vert floats in and out of the beat, allowing the rhythm to do much of the work and creating a record that feels almost impossible to experience sitting still.

Dior — Pop Smoke

“Dior” moves with weight. Sliding bass, sharp percussion and dark production create a menacing backdrop for Pop Smoke’s unmistakably deep voice, which lands as another rhythmic element within the track. The contrast between his controlled delivery and the restless beat gives the record its particular intensity.

Lose Control — Missy Elliott featuring Ciara & Fatman Scoop

“Lose Control” turns controlled chaos into a dance record. Frenetic percussion and electronic production move at a relentless pace while Fatman Scoop’s booming commands raise the intensity even further. Missy Elliott and Ciara glide through the commotion, creating a track whose entire structure seems designed around the physical act of movement.

NUEVAYoL — Bad Bunny

“NUEVAYoL” opens with the warmth of salsa before shifting into a harder, contemporary pulse, immediately establishing the tension between nostalgia and reinvention that drives the record. Drawing from El Gran Combo de Puerto Rico’s “Un Verano en Nueva York,” Bad Bunny folds familiar musical textures into his own rhythmic world. The result feels celebratory and kinetic, with percussion and personality carrying the song forward.

Ruff Ryders’ Anthem — DMX

“Ruff Ryders’ Anthem” gets its power from restraint. Swizz Beatz’s sparse production—built around an instantly recognizable synth line and hard, deliberate drums—creates an open canvas for DMX’s commanding delivery. The chant-like hook turns that intensity outward, transforming the record from an individual performance into something communal.

If I Can’t — 50 Cent

“If I Can’t” pairs Dr. Dre’s muscular, tightly wound production with 50 Cent’s famously unhurried delivery. That contrast gives the record its swagger: the beat pushes forward while 50 sounds completely unfazed by it. The result is controlled rather than chaotic, driven by confidence that never needs to overextend itself.

We Found Love — Rihanna featuring Calvin Harris

“We Found Love” is built around escalation. Calvin Harris begins with a relatively simple electronic framework before synths and percussion steadily expand toward an enormous release. Rihanna’s vocal remains direct and emotionally clear against the increasingly euphoric production, creating the tension that makes each drop land even harder.

Ante Up (Robbin Hood Theory) — M.O.P.

“Ante Up” arrives at full intensity and barely lets up. Built around an urgent sample and pounding drums, the production gives M.O.P.’s explosive delivery an equally aggressive backdrop. Voices, beat and hook all seem to compete for space, creating the kind of controlled overload that makes the track feel perpetually on the verge of boiling over.

Empire State of Mind — JAY-Z featuring Alicia Keys

“Empire State of Mind” balances detailed storytelling with arena-sized release. JAY-Z’s conversational verses move over a steady piano-led beat before Alicia Keys opens the record up with its soaring chorus. That shift in scale—from grounded verses to an expansive hook—is what gives the song its enduring lift, turning reflection into something triumphant.
